_what_this_is: The material voice of every room in this location, in this location's own language. Exported from tools/room-voices.mjs by tools/export-pack.mjs for row 44 step 0; the engine now LOADS this rather than declaring it. Every `why` is the period justification the voice was authored with — a material table with no justification is a preference.

hall_state.why: The great hall is THE display room: oak wainscot with a carved frieze over a flagged floor is the standard c.1660 gentry treatment, and the hall is the one room entitled to armorial glass in quantity.
hall_state.walls: dark oak wall panelling in fielded bays with a carved frieze above it, lime-plastered wall head
hall_state.ceiling: a flat lime-plastered ceiling with moulded plaster ribs
hall_state.floor: a broad worn stone flagstone floor
hall_state.blank: unbroken oak panelling in fielded bays under its carved frieze, with the lime-plastered wall head above it

great_chamber.why: The solar — the great chamber over the hall — is the upper display room and carries the hall's own fabric: oak wainscot and a carved frieze. What it does NOT carry is the arms. Painted heraldry belongs in the hall window, and the ration allows the hall and at most the principal parlour; the prompt lint refuses it anywhere else, which is how this voice was split off from the hall's in the first place.
great_chamber.walls: dark oak wall panelling in fielded bays with a carved frieze above it, lime-plastered wall head
great_chamber.ceiling: a flat lime-plastered ceiling with moulded plaster ribs
great_chamber.blank: unbroken oak panelling in fielded bays under its carved frieze, with the lime-plastered wall head above it

parlour_wainscot.why: Study, library, dining parlour and muniment room are the panelled withdrawing rooms — dark oak wainscot over boards, the voice the approved study reference already carries and the one place it belongs.

parlour_armorial.why: The dining parlour is the principal parlour: identical fabric to the other panelled rooms, but period practice allows it the single shield the great hall's window carries in quantity — and no more.

long_gallery.why: A long gallery is a walking room lit down one whole side: oak wainscot, a boarded floor and ranges of windows rather than single ones, which is why it gets its own voice and not the parlour's.
long_gallery.walls: plain oak wainscot below limewashed plaster, with a moulded oak cornice at the wall head
long_gallery.floor: long wide oak floorboards running the length of the gallery
long_gallery.blank: unbroken oak wainscot below limewashed plaster

bedchamber.why: A c.1660 bedchamber is wainscoted to chair height and HUNG above it — worsted or tapestry hangings, not panelling to the cornice; the best chamber's hangings are the richest in the house.
bedchamber.walls: oak wainscot to chair height with wall hangings above it
bedchamber.blank: unbroken wainscot below and hangings above

hangings.best: a full set of woven tapestry hangings in faded green, umber and dull gold, hung from a rail just below the ceiling and falling to the wainscot capping
hangings.good: hangings of dull red worsted say, hung from a rail below the ceiling and falling to the wainscot capping
hangings.plain: plain hangings of undyed wool serge, hung from a rail below the ceiling and falling to the wainscot capping

garden_parlour.why: There is no orangery and no sash window in 1660: a garden room of this date is a garden PARLOUR — a low-wainscoted room whose one distinction is generous leaded casement bays looking onto the privy garden. Its light comes from casement COUNT, never from a wall of glass.
garden_parlour.walls: light-toned oak wainscot to chair height below limewashed plaster
garden_parlour.floor: a floor of square stone paviours
garden_parlour.blank: unbroken light oak wainscot below limewashed plaster

cross_passage.why: The cross passage is the working spine between hall and service: plain oak wainscot under limewash over flags, worn by traffic — no fielded panelling and no frieze.
cross_passage.walls: plain oak wainscot below limewashed plaster
cross_passage.ceiling: a boarded ceiling of plain oak boards on exposed joists
cross_passage.blank: unbroken plain oak wainscot below limewashed plaster

great_stair.why: The great stair and its landing are shown to guests: a heavy oak newel stair with turned balusters, wainscot to chair height, and the one tall stair window the plan actually draws.
great_stair.walls: oak wainscot to chair height below limewashed plaster
great_stair.blank: unbroken oak wainscot below limewashed plaster

back_stair.why: A back stair is service fabric: limewashed plaster over a PLAIN BOARDED DADO, plain oak treads, no mouldings and no fielded joinery anywhere.
back_stair.walls: limewashed plaster above a plain boarded oak dado of square-edged boards, with no mouldings and no fielded joinery
back_stair.floor: plain scrubbed oak treads and boards
back_stair.blank: unbroken limewash above a plain boarded dado

service.why: Kitchen and buttery in 1660: stone flags, limewashed plaster straight down to the floor, a great open hearth, scrubbed oak fittings. A room where food is dressed carries no joinery on its walls at all — the one horizontal that runs them is the plain peg-rail the gear hangs from.
service.walls: rough limewashed plaster over stone, carried straight down to the floor unbroken by any timber lining, joinery or moulding
service.ceiling: heavy smoke-darkened oak ceiling joists with plain boards between them

servants_hall.why: The servants' hall is the plainest inhabited room in the house: plain limewash, a brick or flag floor, scrubbed oak, and nothing else. Fielded oak joinery here would be a status error, not just a material one.
servants_hall.walls: plain limewashed plaster carried straight down to the floor, unbroken by any timber lining, joinery or moulding
servants_hall.ceiling: plain exposed oak joists with boards between them
servants_hall.floor: a floor of worn red brick laid on edge in straight courses running away from you, every brick a long narrow rectangle end-on, no square pavers and no herringbone

outdoors_walled.why: A privy garden, an entrance court or an approach seen against a wall is OUTSIDE: the wall in frame is garden brick or coursed stone under open sky, with planting and a path underfoot. No interior fabric of any kind belongs in it — this is Kabe's veto, made mechanical.
outdoors_walled.walls: a garden wall of weathered red brick in English bond on a coursed stone plinth, open sky above it
outdoors_walled.walls_with_openings: the manor's own exterior elevation of weathered red brick in English bond, with dressed stone quoins, moulded stone window surrounds and a coursed stone plinth, open sky above the roofline
outdoors_walled.floor: raked gravel paths between low clipped box and turf
outdoors_walled.blank: unbroken weathered brickwork on its stone plinth

outdoors_open.why: A facing the plan types `open` has no wall at all: the view runs out over the forecourt or the park. What closes it and gives the gate its ruler is the low coursed-stone boundary wall that fences a forecourt of this date, its coping at the ruled height.
outdoors_open.walls: no building wall at all: the view runs out over open ground, closed only by a low coursed-stone boundary wall running across the far side of it, under open sky
outdoors_open.floor: raked gravel and worn turf running to the bottom edge of frame
outdoors_open.blank: an unbroken low boundary wall under open sky

chair_rail.line: the wainscot chair-rail above the floor
chair_rail.sentence: A clearly legible wainscot chair-rail runs continuously corner to corner at exactly 0.95 m above the floor, on every exposed wall surface including the side-wall returns.
chair_rail.label: CHAIR-RAIL 0.95 M ABOVE FLOOR - GATE ANCHOR
chair_rail.why: blueprint §11's universal anchor, and the only one the panelled rooms need

dado_capping.line: the plain oak dado capping above the floor
dado_capping.sentence: A plain unmoulded oak capping runs continuously corner to corner at exactly 0.95 m above the floor, topping the boarded dado on every exposed wall surface including the side-wall returns. It is a plain square-edged batten with no mouldings worked on it at all.
dado_capping.label: DADO CAPPING 0.95 M ABOVE FLOOR - GATE ANCHOR
dado_capping.why: a boarded service dado is capped with a plain batten; same height, no mouldings, no panelling

hanging_rail.line: the plain oak hanging rail above the floor
hanging_rail.sentence: A plain scrubbed-oak hanging rail, pegged with iron hooks, runs continuously corner to corner at exactly 0.95 m above the floor, fixed straight onto the limewashed plaster on every exposed wall surface including the side-wall returns. It is a single square-edged batten on bare plaster, with no timber lining, no joinery and no moulding anywhere behind it or below it.
hanging_rail.label: HANGING RAIL 0.95 M ABOVE FLOOR - GATE ANCHOR
hanging_rail.why: the peg-rail every c.1660 kitchen, buttery and servants' hall hung its gear from — a real continuous horizontal in a room that has no wainscot

string_course.line: the stone string-course above the ground
string_course.sentence: A single projecting course of dressed stone runs continuously across the whole wall at exactly 0.95 m above the ground, capping the wall's plinth. It is masonry standing in the open air: no timber rail, no lining and no built interior finish of any kind appears anywhere in this picture.
string_course.label: STRING-COURSE 0.95 M ABOVE GROUND - GATE ANCHOR
string_course.why: a brick garden wall of this date is built off a stone plinth capped by a string-course; it is the outdoor equivalent horizontal

coping.line: the boundary wall coping above the ground
coping.sentence: A low coursed-stone boundary wall runs right across the far side of the view, and the flat stone coping along its top sits at exactly 0.95 m above the ground at that wall. It is masonry standing in the open air: no timber rail, no lining and no built interior finish of any kind appears anywhere in this picture.
coping.label: COPING 0.95 M ABOVE GROUND - GATE ANCHOR
coping.why: an open facing has no building wall; a forecourt of this date is closed by a low walled boundary, and its coping is the one ruled horizontal available

wall/oak-wainscot-with-hangings.note: the DADO band only; the field band above it is one of the three `wall/hangings-*` variants, chosen per room by `hangingsFor`

wall/plain-oak-wainscot-limewash.alias_reason: differ only by "plain" and "to chair height" -- both are oak wainscot below limewashed plaster. THE CONSEQUENCE IS THE POINT: cross_passage had no promoted facing and was the library's only wall swatch; great_stair has one, so this alias turns an ask into a harvest.
wall/plain-oak-wainscot-limewash.note: SWATCH because `cross_passage` has no promoted facing anywhere in the manor -- `hall` is unpainted -- so there is nothing to harvest from

wall/rough-limewash-over-stone.alias_reason: "rough ... over stone" and "plain" are finish adjectives over the same material: limewashed plaster carried straight to the floor with no joinery.

tiling.feature: the trowelled undulation of limewash over rubble
the trowelled undulation of plain limewash

wall/manor-exterior-elevation.note: the THIRTEENTH wall fabric, invisible to a walls/ceiling/floor census: `outdoors_walled.walls_with_openings`, selected in `make-scaffold.mjs` when the plan draws any carrier on that wall line. 7 of the 8 outdoor facings render it

tiling.feature: the weave of undyed wool serge

ceiling/flat-lime-plaster.alias_reason: plain and flat are synonyms here; the material is lime plaster either way.

ceiling/boarded-oak-joists.alias_reason: the same ceiling said twice -- plain oak boards on exposed joists.

ceiling/plain-plastered-soffit.alias_reason: a soffit is where the plaster is, not what it is; plain plaster and plain lime plaster are one material in this period.

floor/broad-stone-flags.alias_reason: broad/large/worn are size adjectives on one material. NO voice's period justification names a different stone or a different laying pattern -- checked, all three say worn stone flags.

tiling.feature: the spread of a broad worn flag

floor/wide-worn-oak-boards.alias_reason: worn is a finish adjective on wide oak floorboards.

floor/gallery-long-oak-boards.alias_reason: "running the length of the gallery" is a LAYING DIRECTION, and direction is already carried by grain_axis room_long, which all three share -- so it is not a second material.
floor/gallery-long-oak-boards.note: the gallery's voice says the boards run its LENGTH, which is what `room_long` means and why grain is a plan fact and not a facing one

tiling.feature: the spread of a worn flag

floor/scrubbed-oak-treads-boards.alias_reason: broad and plain scrubbed are finish adjectives on oak treads and boards. Kept separate from the floorboards: treads name a stair surface.
floor/scrubbed-oak-treads-boards.note: NAMES TWO GEOMETRIES IN ONE STRING -- stair treads and floor boards are not the same surface. Recorded rather than split, because stair rooms are not assembly customers (36-plan.md §2.6)

floor/large-worn-stone-flags.alias_reason: as above: a size adjective, not a different stone.

tiling.feature: the spread of a large worn flag

floor/gravel-and-turf.swatch_prose: raked gravel and worn turf, the two running together

floor/red-brick-on-edge.said: a floor of worn red brick laid on edge
floor/red-brick-on-edge.why: [Kabe, 2026-08-25: "Servants hall has multiple different floor types"] The material alone let one wall lay its bricks as squares beside two laid in courses, so the BOND was named in the voice. Worn red brick laid on edge is the same floor before and after; what the added words rule is how it is laid, which is a finish of the material and not a second material.
